articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than culverts. Residents in Brownsville and Englewood are still sandbagging every summer.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.3 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only 11 of 67 planned drainage projects
Engineering and consulting contracts account for $18.2 million of expenditures while actual construction totals $12.7 million
Brownsville and Englewood neighborhoods, identified as top priorities in 2023, remain without significant infrastructure improvements
articles.body:
The sandbags stacked along Fairfield Drive in Brownsville are sun-bleached now, faded from blue to pale gray. Patricia Hendricks put them there in August 2024. She's added more every hurricane season since.

"They told us three years ago we were priority one," Hendricks said, standing in her carport where a waterline from last September's flooding still marks the drywall. "I'm still waiting to see a single piece of pipe go in the ground."

In November 2023, Escambia County voters approved a stormwater utility fee by a margin of 58 to 42 percent. The fee—$7.50 per month for residential properties, scaled rates for commercial—was sold as the solution to decades of drainage neglect. County commissioners promised shovel-ready projects. They promised relief for neighborhoods that flood during routine afternoon thunderstorms.

Thirty-one months later, the county has collected $47.3 million. It has completed 11 projects.

Where the Money Went

Public records obtained by The Flightline show a stormwater fund heavy on planning and light on construction.

Of the $47.3 million collected through April 2026, the county has spent $38.1 million. The largest category: $18.2 million for engineering studies, hydraulic modeling, consultant contracts and project design. Actual construction accounts for $12.7 million. The remaining $7.2 million covers program administration, equipment and debt service on bonds the county issued against future fee revenue.

The 11 completed projects are concentrated in unincorporated areas north of Interstate 10—Cantonment, Molino, the Beulah corridor. Most involve ditch regrading and pipe replacements. None address the flooding hotspots identified as critical priorities when commissioners pitched the fee to voters.

Brownsville. Englewood. Oakfield. Myrtle Grove. The names appeared in every county presentation in 2023. Three years later, not one has seen construction begin.

The Consultant Question

Escambia County's stormwater program is managed by a skeleton crew: four full-time employees in the Public Works department handle a system spanning 1,200 miles of drainage infrastructure. The county has relied on outside consultants for nearly every function beyond basic maintenance.

The largest contract belongs to Jacobs Engineering, the Dallas-based firm hired in early 2024 to develop a comprehensive stormwater master plan. That contract, initially valued at $4.8 million, has grown through amendments to $7.3 million. The master plan remains in draft form.

"We're building this program from the ground up," said County Administrator Wes Moreno at a May budget workshop. "You can't rush the engineering. If we put in undersized infrastructure, we're back here in ten years doing it again."

Critics say the county is using complexity as cover for inaction.

"They've studied Brownsville's drainage problems four separate times since I've lived here," said Marcus Williams, a resident of West Yonge Street who has documented flooding on his block since 2019. "We don't need another model. We need a culvert that can handle more than a half-inch of rain."

Williams provided The Flightline with county documents showing drainage studies of his neighborhood conducted in 2011, 2017, 2021 and again in 2024 under the new stormwater fee program. Each identified the same choke point: a 36-inch pipe under Fairfield Drive that should be 60 inches. The 2024 study recommended the same fix as the 2011 study.

The project remains in the design phase.

Promises Made

The 2023 campaign for the stormwater fee was unusually specific for a local ballot measure. County staff produced a priority project list with 67 locations, cost estimates and preliminary timelines. Glossy mailers showed flooding photographs next to renderings of new retention ponds. Commissioner Steven Barry, who championed the fee, promised "visible progress within 18 months."

That timeline came and went without comment from county leadership.

Barry did not respond to interview requests for this article. His chief of staff, reached by phone, said the commissioner's position is that "the program is proceeding appropriately given the complexity of the work."

The original 67-project list has been revised twice. The current version, dated February 2026, shows 23 projects in design, 14 in "preliminary engineering," 8 under construction and 11 complete. The remaining 11 have been deferred to a second phase with no timeline attached.

Several deferred projects are in Brownsville and Englewood—the same neighborhoods featured most prominently in the 2023 campaign materials.

A Question of Capacity

Some county officials, speaking on background because they were not authorized to discuss the program publicly, described a department overwhelmed by ambition.

The stormwater fee created a new revenue stream but not a new bureaucracy to manage it. Public Works Director Derek Burkett, who oversees roads, bridges, traffic signals and solid waste in addition to stormwater, has requested additional staffing in each of the past two budget cycles. Each request was partially funded.

The department currently has two project managers handling all 67 stormwater projects alongside their existing workloads. Consultant contracts require county oversight, review and approval at multiple stages. The bottleneck is not money. It's bandwidth.

"You can hire all the consultants you want," one county employee said. "Someone still has to review their work. Someone has to go to the meetings. Someone has to sign off. We don't have the bodies."

Moreno, the county administrator, acknowledged staffing constraints but rejected the premise that the program is failing.

"We're three years into a 20-year program," Moreno said. "The infrastructure we're building will serve this community for 50 years. I understand the frustration, but this is how major capital programs work."

What Residents See

Patricia Hendricks is not interested in 20-year timelines. She is 71 years old. She has lived in Brownsville since 1988. She has replaced her flooring three times.

The flooding in her neighborhood follows a predictable pattern. Rain falls. Water sheets across Fairfield Drive. It backs up behind inadequate drainage. It enters homes on the south side of the street, where elevations are slightly lower. The water recedes within hours, leaving mud and debris and the particular smell of saturated drywall.

"My insurance won't cover it anymore," Hendricks said. "They say it's repetitive loss. They dropped me."

She now carries a flood policy through the National Flood Insurance Program, though her property is not in a designated flood zone. The premium is $2,400 annually. Combined with the stormwater fee, she is paying roughly $2,500 per year for a problem the county has promised to fix since before she moved in.

Hendricks attended the Board of County Commissioners meeting on June 3. She was one of four Brownsville residents who spoke during public comment. She brought photographs. She brought her documentation of past studies. She asked when construction would begin.

Commissioner Barry was not present. The remaining commissioners listened, thanked her for her input and moved to the next agenda item.

The sandbags are still on Fairfield Drive. Hurricane season started June 1.

articles.headline: Who Owns the Lots Behind Cordova Mall? A Private Equity Trail From Pensacola to Phoenix
articles.dek: Fourteen acres sat empty for six years while ownership changed hands through a maze of LLCs. Now a 280-unit apartment complex is moving forward—and neighbors say they were never notified.
brief: Empty lots behind Cordova Mall have changed hands through at least seven LLCs since 2020, with ultimate ownership tracing to a Phoenix-based private equity firm managing over $2 billion in assets.
Escambia County property records show the land was assessed at $1.2 million in 2020 but sold for $8.4 million in 2024—a 600% increase with no improvements made.
Residents of the adjacent Carrington Lane subdivision say they received no notice of the proposed 280-unit development despite county code requiring notification within 300 feet.
articles.body:
The chain-link fence went up sometime in March. Nobody in the Carrington Lane subdivision remembers exactly when. One morning the rusted posts just appeared along the tree line, orange survey flags fluttering in the wind where kids used to cut through to the mall.

"We figured somebody was finally doing something with it," said Marcus Webb, who has lived on Carrington Lane for eleven years. "But nobody told us what."

What somebody is doing: a 280-unit luxury apartment complex called The Meridian at Cordova, according to site plans filed with Escambia County in April. Three four-story buildings. A clubhouse. A dog park. Underground parking.

The developer listed on the permit application is Meridian Pensacola Holdings LLC. The company was registered with the Florida Division of Corporations on February 3, 2026. Its registered agent is a law firm in Tallahassee. Its principal address is a UPS Store mailbox in Scottsdale, Arizona.

Behind that LLC is another. And another. And another.

Following the Paper Trail

The fourteen acres behind Cordova Mall have been vacant since 2018, when a Sears Auto Center and adjacent outparcels were demolished. For six years, the land sat empty—a scrubby expanse of saw palmetto and slash pine sandwiched between the mall's loading docks and the backyards of Carrington Lane.

Escambia County property records show the parcel changed hands five times between January 2020 and August 2024. Each buyer was a limited liability company. None of the LLCs shared an obvious name or address with the previous owner.

The Flightline spent three weeks tracing ownership through corporate filings in Florida, Delaware, Arizona, and Nevada. The trail:

January 2020: Cordova Retail Partners LLC purchases the land from Seritage Growth Properties, the REIT that inherited former Sears locations. Sale price: $1.2 million. Cordova Retail Partners is registered in Delaware. Its sole member is listed as CRP Manager Inc., also Delaware.

September 2021: The property transfers to Gulf South Land Acquisitions LLC, a Florida company. Sale price: $2.1 million. Gulf South's registered agent is a corporate service company in Miami. Its manager is listed as GSLA Holdings Inc.—incorporated in Nevada, with a registered address that matches a virtual office provider in Las Vegas.

March 2023: Gulf South sells to Emerald Coast Development Fund II LLC. Price: $4.8 million. Emerald Coast is registered in Florida but managed by ECDF GP LLC, a Delaware entity. ECDF GP's corporate documents list a single member: Ridgeline Capital Partners LP.

August 2024: The property moves to 9th Avenue Ventures LLC for $8.4 million. 9th Avenue Ventures is managed by the same Tallahassee law firm that would later register Meridian Pensacola Holdings.

Ridgeline Capital Partners is where the trail surfaces into daylight. The firm is headquartered in Phoenix and manages what its website describes as "over $2 billion in opportunistic real estate investments across the Sun Belt." Its portfolio includes apartment complexes, self-storage facilities, and retail centers in Texas, Florida, Georgia, and Arizona.

Phone calls and emails to Ridgeline's Phoenix office were not returned. A receptionist who answered on June 6 said the firm does not comment on individual investments.

The 600% Question

Between 2020 and 2024, the assessed value of the Cordova lots increased from $1.2 million to $3.1 million, according to the Escambia County Property Appraiser. The actual sale prices suggest the market saw something the tax rolls didn't.

The land sold for $1.2 million in 2020, $2.1 million in 2021, $4.8 million in 2023, and $8.4 million in 2024. That's a 600% increase in four years—on property where nothing was built, no rezoning occurred, and no infrastructure improvements were made.

"That's not unusual for speculative land transactions," said Dr. Patricia Odom, a real estate economist at the University of West Florida. "You're not paying for what's there. You're paying for what you think you can do with it."

What made the land valuable? Odom pointed to several factors: proximity to Cordova Mall and Interstate 10, the multifamily housing shortage across Northwest Florida, and Escambia County's relatively permissive approach to density in commercial corridors.

The parcel is zoned C-2, commercial general. Under Escambia County's land development code, multifamily residential is a permitted use in C-2 zones, subject to site plan review. No rezoning hearing required. No vote by the Board of County Commissioners.

"It's an administrative approval," said County Planning Director Harold Simmons in an interview. "If the site plan meets the code requirements, we approve it."

The Notice That Wasn't

Escambia County Code Section 3.08.03 requires written notice to property owners within 300 feet of any proposed development requiring site plan review. The notice must be mailed at least 14 days before the review date.

The Flightline contacted twelve homeowners on Carrington Lane whose properties fall within 300 feet of the Cordova lots. All twelve said they received no notice of the Meridian at Cordova development. Six provided copies of their mail logs from the relevant time period—a service offered by USPS called Informed Delivery—showing no correspondence from Escambia County Development Services.

"First I heard about it was when my neighbor showed me the fence," said Patricia Drummond, whose backyard shares a property line with the site. "Then I went online and found the site plan. Two hundred eighty apartments. Four stories. Twenty feet from my fence line."

Simmons, the planning director, said notification records showed notices were mailed on April 2 to 47 addresses. He declined to provide copies of the mailing list, citing an ongoing internal review.

"If there was a discrepancy in notification, we take that seriously," Simmons said. "We're looking into it."

The site plan review occurred on April 18. Meeting minutes show no members of the public spoke during the comment period. The plan was approved unanimously by the Development Review Committee.

Who Profits?

The ownership structure of the Cordova lots—multiple LLCs layered across multiple states—is not illegal. It's not even unusual in commercial real estate. But it serves specific purposes, according to experts.

"The LLC structure provides liability protection," said Jonathan Kemp, a real estate attorney in Pensacola who is not involved in the Cordova project. "If something goes wrong with the development, creditors can only go after the assets inside that specific LLC, not the parent company's other holdings."

The multi-state layering offers additional benefits. Delaware LLCs are not required to disclose their members publicly. Nevada has no state corporate income tax. Arizona has favorable pass-through tax treatment for real estate partnerships.

"It's a tax efficiency play," said Dr. Odom. "And a privacy play. You can own half of downtown and nobody knows it's you unless they're willing to dig through corporate filings in four states."

The Flightline's review of Escambia County property records found at least 23 other parcels with ownership structures involving the same Tallahassee law firm that represents Meridian Pensacola Holdings. The parcels include two other vacant lots in the Cordova Mall vicinity, a former car dealership on Mobile Highway, and several acres near the new Amazon distribution center on Highway 29.

Whether those properties share ultimate ownership with the Cordova lots could not be determined from public records.

What Happens Next

The Meridian at Cordova site plan approval is valid for 18 months. Construction must begin by October 2027 or the approval expires.

Building permit applications have not yet been filed. Grading permits were approved on May 30. Heavy equipment appeared on site the first week of June.

Residents of Carrington Lane have requested a meeting with County Commissioner Doug Underhill, whose district includes the area. Underhill's office confirmed the meeting request was received but has not scheduled a date.

"We're not saying don't build apartments," said Webb, the eleven-year resident. "We're saying tell us about it. Knock on our door. Send a letter. Something."

He stood at his back fence on a recent afternoon, watching a surveyor plant another orange flag near the tree line. A mockingbird sat on the chain-link, unbothered.

"Six years we looked at those woods," Webb said. "Now we're going to look at somebody's balcony."

The Flightline submitted public records requests to Escambia County for all notification documentation related to the Meridian at Cordova site plan. A response is due by June 28. This story will be updated as additional information becomes available.

articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Draws 400,000 Visitors. The Beach Road Can't Handle It.
articles.dek: Pensacola Beach's single access point becomes a parking lot every July. After last year's four-hour backups, county officials are floating a reservation system—and locals are furious.
brief: Last July's Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show created four-hour traffic delays on the Bob Sikes Bridge, stranding thousands of visitors and residents
Escambia County is considering a beach reservation system that would limit vehicle access during major events, drawing sharp opposition from residents and business owners
With the 2026 show five weeks away, officials remain deadlocked on solutions while projecting this year's attendance could exceed 450,000
articles.body:
The line of brake lights started at the foot of the Bob Sikes Bridge and stretched back past the Walmart on Gulf Breeze Parkway. It was 2 p.m. on July 12, 2025. The Blue Angels wouldn't fly for another three hours.

Sarah Mitchum sat in her Honda Pilot with two kids in car seats, the AC struggling against 94-degree heat, watching the same palm tree outside her window for forty-five minutes. She'd left her home in East Hill at noon for what Google Maps promised would be a thirty-seven-minute drive. She arrived at her rental on Via de Luna at 6:15 p.m. The show was over.

"We paid $1,200 for that weekend," Mitchum said. "My kids saw the planes from the car. That was our Blue Angels experience."

She was one of roughly 400,000 people who attempted to reach Pensacola Beach during last year's homecoming week, according to Escambia County estimates. The Bob Sikes Bridge—the only vehicle access point to the island—has a theoretical capacity of 1,800 vehicles per hour under ideal conditions. On the Saturday of the air show, traffic counts showed more than 4,200 vehicles attempting to cross during the peak afternoon window.

The math doesn't work. It hasn't worked for years. And with the 2026 Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show scheduled for July 10-11, county officials are running out of time to find a solution that doesn't exist.

One Road In, One Road Out

Pensacola Beach sits on Santa Rosa Island, a narrow barrier strip separating Pensacola Bay from the Gulf of Mexico. The Bob Sikes Bridge, completed in 1960, connects the island to Gulf Breeze across the Intracoastal Waterway. For sixty-six years, it has been the only way to drive onto or off of the beach.

The bridge carries roughly 15,000 vehicles on a typical summer Saturday. During Blue Angels week, that number can triple.

"The infrastructure was built for a different era," said Marcus Webb, Escambia County's director of public works. "We're trying to move 21st-century crowds through a 1960s bottleneck."

A second bridge has been discussed for decades. Studies were commissioned in 1987, 1994, 2008 and 2019. Each concluded that a new crossing—either from Pensacola directly to the island or a second span parallel to Bob Sikes—would cost between $180 million and $340 million depending on the route. No funding has ever been allocated.

The most recent proposal, a bridge from the foot of 17th Avenue in Pensacola to the western end of the island near Fort Pickens, was rejected by the Santa Rosa Island Authority in 2021. Members cited environmental concerns and opposition from residents who feared increased development.

"A second bridge doesn't solve traffic," said SRIA board member Catherine Holt at the time. "It just brings more cars."

The Reservation Question

With construction off the table, Escambia County Administrator Wes Moreno floated a different approach at a commission workshop in April: a reservation system that would require visitors to book vehicle access to the beach during major events.

Under the proposal, drivers would reserve time slots through a county website. Only vehicles with confirmed reservations would be allowed across the bridge during designated hours. Residents with proof of address would be exempt. So would commercial vehicles and hotel guests with confirmation numbers.

"We're not talking about limiting access to the beach," Moreno said at the April 17 workshop. "We're talking about managing flow so people can actually get there."

The system would be modeled on reservation programs at Muir Woods National Monument and Rocky Mountain National Park, which have used timed-entry permits since 2018 and 2020 respectively. Both parks reported reduced crowding and shorter wait times after implementation.

Pensacola Beach, however, is not a national park.

The proposal drew immediate opposition from the Santa Rosa Island Authority, the Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce and the Gulf Breeze City Council, which passed a resolution on May 4 calling the plan "an unconstitutional restriction on the free movement of citizens."

"You're telling taxpayers they need permission to use public roads," said Gulf Breeze Mayor Cherry Fitch. "That's not traffic management. That's rationing."

Business Owners Caught in the Middle

On a Tuesday morning in early June, the parking lot at Flounder's Chowder House was empty except for a delivery truck unloading kegs. General manager Tony Raines stood on the deck overlooking the sound, watching a single kayaker paddle past.

"This is what June looks like," he said. "July is different."

Flounder's is one of the oldest restaurants on Pensacola Beach, open since 1979. Raines has managed it for eighteen years. He estimates that Blue Angels week accounts for 8-12% of the restaurant's annual revenue, compressed into seven days.

"Those tourists sitting in traffic last year? They weren't eating at my restaurant," he said. "They weren't spending money anywhere. They were sitting in their cars."

Raines said he's open to ideas that would keep traffic moving but worried that a reservation system would scare visitors away entirely.

"People don't plan beach trips around government websites," he said. "They just go somewhere else."

Down the road at the Hampton Inn, front desk supervisor Maria Delgado said the hotel fielded more than sixty complaints during last year's air show weekend, mostly from guests who missed dinner reservations or couldn't reach the beach in time for the show.

"We had people crying in the lobby," she said. "They'd driven from Atlanta, from Birmingham, from New Orleans. And they couldn't get to the room they'd booked months earlier."

The hotel has already sold out for this year's show. Delgado said management is considering offering guests the option to check in the day before and stay through traffic rather than attempt a same-day arrival.

The Sheriff's Gamble

For the past eleven years, the Escambia County Sheriff's Office has managed traffic flow during Blue Angels weekend using a system of rolling closures and manual intersection control. Deputies are stationed at key points along Gulf Breeze Parkway and Via de Luna, directing traffic by hand.

Last year, the sheriff's office deployed 143 personnel to the beach over the two-day event—the largest traffic detail in department history. It wasn't enough.

"We had units at every intersection from the toll booth to Park West," said Captain James Thornton, who oversaw the operation. "The problem isn't the intersections. It's the bridge."

Thornton said the department is considering a more aggressive approach for 2026: closing the Bob Sikes Bridge to inbound traffic entirely during peak hours and running a mandatory shuttle system from remote parking lots on the mainland.

"If we can't control the flow of cars, we control whether there are cars at all," he said.

The shuttle proposal would use the Pensacola Bay Center parking structure and a vacant lot near the foot of the Three Mile Bridge as staging areas. Buses would run every ten to fifteen minutes, with a $20 per person round-trip fare to offset costs.

Sheriff Chip Simmons has not publicly endorsed the plan. A spokesperson said the department is "evaluating all options" and will make an announcement by late June.

Residents Draw a Line

The Beach Community Church on Via de Luna Drive holds Sunday services at 9 a.m. and 11 a.m., year-round. During air show weekend, some members have arrived as early as 6 a.m. to guarantee a parking spot.

"We've had people tell us they slept in their cars Saturday night so they wouldn't miss church Sunday," said Pastor David Renfroe. "That's not an exaggeration."

Renfroe is among roughly 3,200 year-round residents of Pensacola Beach—people who live, work, and vote on an island that swells to ten times its population during peak season. Many of them bought property specifically for the quiet months, the empty beaches of November through April.

They knew what they were signing up for. But they're tired of being stuck on the wrong side of the bridge.

Carol Whitfield has lived in a condo on Quietwater Beach since 2014. Last July, she drove to Publix in Gulf Breeze for groceries on a Thursday afternoon. The round trip took three hours and forty minutes.

"I'm seventy-two years old," she said. "I had ice cream in the car. What was I supposed to do?"

Whitfield supports the reservation system—"anything that keeps some of these cars off the road"—but says she's in the minority among her neighbors.

"People around here have this idea that restrictions are a slippery slope," she said. "If you let them limit traffic during air show week, pretty soon they'll be limiting it on Memorial Day. Then every weekend. Then you need a pass to live in your own home."

She paused.

"I understand the fear. I just don't think it's realistic."

The Clock Is Ticking

The Escambia County Commission will hold a public hearing on traffic management proposals on June 23. Staff recommendations are due by June 30. The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show begins July 10.

That leaves roughly two weeks to implement whatever solution the commission selects—assuming they select anything at all.

At last Thursday's commission meeting, the five members spent forty-five minutes discussing the traffic issue without reaching any conclusions. Commissioner Steven Barry said he remained "skeptical" of the reservation system. Commissioner Lumon May called for more study. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh suggested that the Navy, which stages the air show, should bear more responsibility for traffic management.

"This is their event," Bergosh said. "They're the ones drawing 400,000 people to a beach that holds about 50,000 comfortably."

A spokesperson for Naval Air Station Pensacola declined to comment on traffic management, calling it "a county matter."

Meanwhile, the Blue Angels practice schedule continues. Every Tuesday and Wednesday through the summer, the six F/A-18 Super Hornets scream over Pensacola Bay in formation, banking hard over the lighthouse, trailing white smoke against blue sky.

From the deck at Flounder's, Tony Raines can see them perfectly. So can the lunch crowd, necks craned back, phones pointed up.

"People love those planes," he said. "They'll put up with a lot to see them."

He watched a tight diamond formation roll west toward Perdido Key.

"The question is how much."
